# QM Intermediate: Course overview {#intermediate-course}

QM Intermediate builds on the probability, inference, and R skills from QM
Basic. The central question changes from "What does this sample show?" to
"How is an outcome related to several variables at the same time?"

For a founder these are the questions behind most decisions. How much extra
revenue does one extra euro of advertising bring? Does a lower price sell
more, once you take the season into account? Does the new version of your
website sell more than the old one? Such questions are most commonly
answered with regression analysis, in R or with an AI assistant. This
course teaches you to read regression output, to check it, and to make
decisions with it.

::: {.outcomes}
<span class="label">By the end of QM Intermediate, you can</span>

- formulate simple and multiple-regression questions from E&BI problems
- fit, diagnose, and interpret linear regression models in R
- distinguish a coefficient, fitted value, residual, and confidence
  interval
- interpret t-tests of coefficients, $R^2$, and overall and partial F-tests
- use dummy variables, interaction terms, and quadratic terms, and tell a
  moderator from a mediator
- analyse an A/B test and a one-way ANOVA with a regression on dummy variables
- explain how control variables change an estimate without automatically
  making it causal
- read the main regression results in a business or management paper.
:::

## The data we use

All lectures use the Shark Tank teaching file. One row is one pitch on the
US television show *Shark Tank*: 1,441 pitches from Seasons 1 to 16.
Founders ask a panel of investors, the sharks, for money in exchange for a
share of their company. The file records what the founders asked for, the
share they offered, and whether a deal was agreed on air and on which terms.
Examples and tasks that use the Shark Tank file carry this tag: [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag}.

- The variables are listed in
  [Basic Lecture 1, "The variables in the Shark Tank file"](../basic/b01-introduction-data-analysis.qmd#b01-variable-table).
- The [welcome page](../index.qmd) describes where the data come from and
  what they cannot show: these are selected television pitches, not a random
  sample of all ventures.
- Lectures 1 to 3 study valuations, in millions of dollars: the valuation a
  founder claims and the valuation agreed on air. From Lecture 4 on, the
  outcome is the equity offered, in percent, and the requested amount is
  measured in thousands of dollars.

No other file is needed for the lectures. Some examples use small invented
datasets that the code on the page creates. The mock exam uses a second,
invented dataset that you download from its page.

## What this course builds on

QM Intermediate uses a small set of ideas from QM Basic. Each row of the
table says where this book explains the idea, so you can look it up when a
lecture uses it.

| Idea | Used here for | Where to read it again |
|---|---|---|
| Mean, variance, standard deviation | slopes, residual spread | [Basic Lecture 3](../basic/b03-discrete-distributions.qmd) |
| Covariance, correlation, conditional mean | the slope formula, what a regression line estimates | [Basic Lecture 5](../basic/b05-joint-covariance-correlation.qmd) |
| Sample and population, estimator and estimate | $\hat\beta_1$ as an estimate of $\beta_1$ | [Basic Lecture 7](../basic/b07-samples-estimators.qmd) |
| Standard error | the "Std. Error" column of R output | [Basic Lecture 8](../basic/b08-sampling-distributions.qmd) |
| Confidence interval, t distribution | intervals for coefficients | [Basic Lecture 9](../basic/b09-t-confidence-intervals.qmd) |
| p-value, test of a claimed value | the "t value" and "Pr(>\|t\|)" columns | [Basic Lecture 10](../basic/b10-testing-errors-power.qmd) |

The preparation for Lecture 1 has a warm-up on five quantities from the last
four rows: estimate, standard error, t statistic, p-value, and confidence
interval.

### If you took QM Basic before 2026

If you took the earlier version of QM Basic, you know the ideas in the table.
Three points are different in this book.

- **Values come from R, not from tables.** Where you looked up a z or t
  table, this book uses `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, and `qt()`. In this book, the
  values you need are given in the task or come from R.
- **Notation for critical values.** You may know $z_{\alpha/2}$ and
  $t_{\alpha/2;\,n-1}$. This book writes $z_{0.975}=1.96$ and
  $t_{0.975,\,df}$, the way R does: `qnorm(0.975)` and `qt(0.975, df)`. The
  numbers are the same.
- **Tests compare with a claimed value.** A test of "the mean equals 15"
  compares $\mu$ with 15 directly, in five steps: hypotheses, test
  statistic, critical value and rejection region, observed value,
  conclusion. Regression output tests every coefficient against the value
  zero in the same way. All tests in this course are two-sided.

It is worth reading the lecture material of
[Basic Lecture 9](../basic/b09-t-confidence-intervals.qmd) and
[Basic Lecture 10](../basic/b10-testing-errors-power.qmd) before the course
starts. The [welcome page](../index.qmd) explains the parts of a chapter,
and [How to succeed in this course](../resources/how-to-succeed.qmd)
shows what a week looks like.

## Course sequence

| Chapter | Main focus |
|---|---|
| Lecture 1 | Simple linear regression. What line best summarises the relationship between two variables? |
| Lecture 2 | What the model assumes and how residuals reveal it. What does the model assume, and what do its residuals show? |
| Lecture 3 | Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test. How precise are the coefficients, and is the model useful at all? |
| Tutorial 1 | Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness |
| Lecture 4 | Multiple regression and what controls do. How do you interpret one predictor while holding others fixed? |
| Lecture 5 | Categories as predictors and joint tests. How do categories enter a model, how do you read an A/B test, and are terms jointly significant? |
| Lecture 6 | Interactions and curvature. When does a slope depend on another variable or change across $x$, and what is a moderator or a mediator? |
| Tutorial 2 | Multiple regression and extensions |
| Code sheet | R commands and formulas for the exam, provided at the exam |
| Mock exam | 100-point practice exam on the whole course |

External video explanations come from Stanford's
[Statistical Learning series](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLoROMvodv4rOzrYsAxzQyHb8n_RWNuS1e).
The supporting textbook is James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani,
*An Introduction to Statistical Learning*, 2nd edition, especially Chapter 3.
For a more formal treatment, consult
[Nieuwenhuis, *Statistical Methods for Business and Economics*](https://tilburguniversity.on.worldcat.org/oclc/317545871),
especially Chapters 19--22. Each lecture chapter contains the definitions,
notation, examples, and practice required for this course.

## The weekly rhythm

There is one lecture per week. In weeks 45 and 48, there is also a tutorial
on the day after the lecture. The [How to succeed in this course](../resources/how-to-succeed.qmd)
page lays out the week with printable checklists.

Bring a charged laptop to every lecture, with RStudio and the R project
for this course open. All code shown in the lecture is in the chapter, ready
to copy. You can run each step yourself and get the same numbers and
figures on your own screen.

## Tutorials and assessment

Two tutorials, one after Lecture 3 and one after Lecture 6, combine
interpretation with practical work in R. If you have forgotten how an R
workflow goes, return to the [R Refresher](../resources/r-refresher.qmd) or the earlier
[Programming for E&BI](https://walshc.github.io/ebi-prog/) textbook.

The QM Intermediate exam lasts 120 minutes in TestVision. You may use
RStudio, Excel, a calculator, and the code sheet. All exam questions are
open questions, and you write your answers in TestVision. The
[QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) is provided at the exam. Use it
during the tutorials too, so that you know where everything is.

The [QM Intermediate Mock Exam](mock-exam.qmd) is available from the first week.
Look at it early to get an impression of what an exam in this course can
look like. After Tutorial 2, work through it
in R. There is also a practice exam in TestVision
itself. It appears in your TestVision account when the lecturer publishes it. You log in with your
university account, and there is no separate link. The university explains
TestVision for students
[on this page](https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/students/studying/exams/e-assessment/testvision).

## Tilly, the course AI assistant

This course has its own chatbot: [Tilly for QM Intermediate](https://chatbot.tilburg.ai/).
It can answer organisational questions, such as questions about the schedule
or about how the grade is calculated. It can also act as a personal tutor
when you solve tasks. You can also ask it to generate additional practice
questions to prepare for the exam. When you use Tilly, follow the steps
Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain on the [welcome page](../index.qmd#working-with-ai).

[Continue to Lecture 1: Simple linear regression](i01-simple-linear-regression.qmd).
